title: CLAY CITY BURGLARY
full_story:
On Sunday at approximately 3:00pm, Wayne County Sheriff’s Deputies took a report of a burglary of a residence in a Rural Clay City located inside Wayne County.  A suspect was developed, Evan Bloehs, 36, of Clay City.  With the assistance of the Richland County Sheriff’s Office Bloehs was located at a hotel in Olney, and was found to be in possession of approximately $5,000 worth of stolen property from the Wayne County residence.

Wayne County Deputies transported Bloehs to the Wayne County Jail.  The stolen property was also retrieved pending transferring back to the owner.

Bloehs faces charges of Residential Burglary, Theft over $500, and Criminal Damage to Property.

title: REDUCED RATE LABS
full_story:

title: TELECOMMUNICATOR’S WEEK
full_story:
National Telecommunicator’s Week runs through Saturday.  National Public Safety Telecommunicator Week is observed every year during the second full week in April.

National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week was originally introduced to Congress in 1991 as a means of honoring everyone who works in public safety telecommunications.  Historically, the week has been marked by a letter from the President of the United States congratulating the dedicated and hard-working individuals who work in public safety telecommunications.

This week is an important reminder of how essential 9-1-1 call takers, police, fire and EMS dispatchers, and related support staff are to public safety.

The following 9-1-1 Telecommunicators are recognized for their dedication and service:

Jennifer Brown has been with the Flora Police Department since the year 2000 and was promoted to Supervisor in 2004.  She came to the Department with a degree in Law Enforcement.  In 2005 she took over the roll as 9-1-1 Coordinator for the County.  She also became an EMT-B (again) in 2018, and has been a member of the Flora Clay County ESDA Unit since 1991.

Michael Dickerson began his career at the Flora Police Department in 2009.  He came to the Department with a degree in Law Enforcement and was an EMT-B for Clay County Hospital.  Michael has also been a member of the Flora Clay County ESDA Unit since 2003.

Nancy Dehart began her career with the Flora Police Department in 2018.  Most will still recognize her voice as she worked for Golden Circle Nutrient Center for many years.

Billy Laughlin began his career with the Flora Police Department in 2020 and joined Flora Clay County ESDA in 2021.

Jennifer Wainscott joined the Flora Police Dept in August of 2023.  She worked for many years in customer service and management industry.

Dispatchers are the unsung heroes of Public Safety and are often referred to as the 1st, first responder to be on scene.  They are there in your time of need, dial 9-1-1 for Police, Fire, and Medical and they will answer your calls 24 x 7 x 365.

Most people that call 9-1-1 do so on their worst day and don’t understand why they ask so many questions.  They do so in order to get the best help to you in a safe and timely manner.

Please remember that if you accidentally call 9-1-1, don’t hang up, stay on the line and explain what happened.  If you hang up, the 9-1-1 dispatcher will be calling you back in order to verify if there is an emergency or not.  If you are having a controlled burn, please call in on the non-emergency line to let the 911 dispatchers know so they don’t send out fire department to put out the fire.  Another request from 9-1-1 is please do not let your child play with your phone as it is so easy for them to accidentally dial 9-1-1, when they hear a voice, they hang up.  Parents, please don’t get mad at the child for calling 9-1-1 explain to them the dos and don’ts of 9-1-1.

For non-emergency calls in the City of Flora call 618-662-9111  For non-emergency calls elsewhere in Clay County call 618-665-3316.

title: WOMAN’S CONFERENCE
full_story:
The Southeastern Illinois Regional Women’s Conference will take place on Friday at the Brubeck Arts Theater at Wabash Valley College in Mt. Carmel.  This regional event brings together women from across Southeastern Illinois for a day of inspiration, professional development, and meaningful connections.

Hosted through a collaboration of several area chambers, including the Flora Chamber of Commerce, Wabash County Chamber, Wayne County Chamber, Carmi Chamber, Lawrence County Chamber, Albion Area Chamber, Robinson Chamber, and Richland County Chamber, the conference is designed to empower women in business, leadership, and the community.

Attendees can expect an engaging experience focused on personal growth, professional development, and networking with women from across the region.  Events like this provide valuable opportunities to learn from others, share experiences, and build relationships that support both individual and community success.

If you would like to attend the conference or learn more about sponsorship opportunities, please reach out to the Flora Chamber of Commerce.

Tickets are $50 per person.  Includes breakfast, boxed lunch, goodie bag, and presentation.  Student Tickets are $20.

title: CROP PROGRESS AND CONDITION
full_story:
Spring has sprung and fields are opening for corn and soybean planting, especially in the southern third of the state.  The USDA says 4% of the corn crop has been planted and 7% of the soybeans.

According to the USDA there were 4.2 days suitable for fieldwork in the week ending April 12th.  Statewide, the average temperature was 51.3 degrees, 1.3 degrees above normal.  Precipitation averaged .25 inches, .51 inches below normal.  Topsoil moisture supply was rated 7% very short, 19% short, 67% adequate, and 7% surplus.  Subsoil moisture supply was rated 10% very short, 28% short, 57% adequate, and 5% surplus.

Corn planted reached 4% as compared to the 5-year average of 3%.

Soybeans planted reached 7% as compared to the 5-year average of 2%.

Winter wheat condition was rated 2% very poor, 4% poor, 27% fair, 57% good, and 10% excellent.  Winter wheat headed is at 6% as compared to the 5-year average of 3%.

title: UIS STRIKE
full_story:
A strike by faculty members at the University of Illinois Springfield has entered its second week as the union and administration remained divided over salary increases.

The two sides have been unable to reach an agreement over salary increases despite the help of a federal mediator and eight bargaining sessions having taken place between tenured and tenure-track faculty since the strike began on April 3rd.

The UIS United Faculty union is seeking a 2.6% increase in the current fiscal year and 6% over the next two years, according to the university’s bargaining update.  UIS has offered three options for increases, two of which begin with 1% raises that could increase under the University of Illinois system’s University Salary Program.

The university said it believes sticking with the program is more financially feasible and told students in an email last month that the institution was running a $19 million deficit.  Powell countered that union contracts at UIS and the other U of I universities show UIS can offer raises that are better than what is set annually by the Board of Trustees for the program.  He added the union is also seeking to guarantee raises will be higher than 1%.

Not all faculty members in the union are participating in the strike.  Some professors are covered under a different collective bargaining agreement, meaning classes are continuing for many students.

The two sides have reached a tentative agreement on parking and professional development.  It would keep a cap on parking fees in place and allow faculty members to roll over funds to future years that are made available to them each year to attend conferences.

A staff union at UIS is also negotiating a new contract and has authorized a strike but have so far not instituted a work stoppage.

title: AWAITING PRITZKER DECISION
full_story:
It’s now up to Illinois Governor JB Pritzker to decide if the state should opt in to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Program.

Illinois voters in 31 counties voted on a non-binding education funding referendum during the March 17th primary election.  The referendum was meant to gauge interest in the program, which aims to incentivize donors to cover costs for private or public school students.

There is no word yet on when or if Pritzker might opt Illinois into the program, but the majority of voters who weighed in on the question want to see it happen.

Sixty-three percent of voters are in favor of Illinois joining the program.  The program would allow private donations to be made to scholarship granting organizations, or SGOs.  Those funds would then be distributed to either public or private school students.

In return, donors would receive up to $1,700 in matching federal tax credit.

Mailee Smith, vice president of policy and litigation at Illinois Policy and an advocate for the program, said it’s an answer to educators’ cries for help.

“We know that there’s a lot of academic need in this state.  We know that school districts and teachers unions, they’ve been clamoring for more funding for education,” she explained.  “And this is an answer.  This is an answer that will not cost the state any money, but it will allow taxpayers to donate directly into their local communities through these scholarship granting organizations.”

Eligible students can receive financial assistance from the program to pay for books, tutoring, college admission exam fees, educational therapy and more.

To qualify for aid from an SGO, a student’s household income must be less than 300% of the area’s median gross income.

Some opponents of the program said it is effectively a voucher program and would bypass public schools to assist private schools, but Smith said it would not redirect any current state or federal funding away from public schools.

The program relies entirely on donations, and some SGOs have already indicated they will direct funds received to public schools according to Smith.

“There is no cost to the state if we don’t do this, but there’s significant missed opportunity if we opt out, and I think the voters get that and they’re telling Gov. Pritzker that they want the state to opt in to this program,” she said.

Pritzker has until the end of the year to opt Illinois in to the program, which takes effect January 1st.  28 states have already opted into the program.
